hints: Start by identifying the reaction type, think about what aqueous NaOH does to a primary halogenoalkane like 1-bromobutane.
Remember that bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so consider what charge the C-Br carbon carries and what species $\text{OH}^-$ is.
For a primary halogenoalkane, decide whether a full carbocation forms first or whether the nucleophile attacks directly as the bond breaks.
walkthrough:
**Identify the reaction**

This is nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane to make an alcohol. Aqueous NaOH provides the nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Look at the C-Br bond polarity**

Br is more electronegative than C, so the bond is polar. Carbon gets a partial positive charge, $\delta+$, and bromine gets $\delta-$.

$$\text{C}^{\delta+} - \text{Br}^{\delta-}$$

**Choose SN2 for a primary halogenoalkane**

1-bromobutane is primary, so it reacts mainly by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$. There is no stable carbocation step. The $\text{OH}^-$ nucleophile attacks the $\delta+$ carbon directly while the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically at the same time.

**Rule out radicals and carbocations**

Homolytic fission would make radicals, which belongs to free radical reactions, not this ionic substitution. A full carbocation intermediate would be $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$, which is favoured by tertiary, not primary, halogenoalkanes.

options.A: Correct. The $\text{OH}^-$ nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to the electron-deficient $\delta+$ carbon in a direct SN2 attack, with heterolytic breaking of the C-Br bond to give $\text{Br}^-$.
options.B: Incorrect. Although C-Br breaking is heterolytic, there is no separate carbocation attacked by the nucleophile here. That describes SN1, which is very slow for primary 1-bromobutane.
options.C: Incorrect. Homolytic fission forms radicals with one electron each, not ions. Also $\text{OH}^-$ is a nucleophile, not an electrophile, and no carbanion is formed in this reaction.
options.D: Incorrect. It mixes two wrong ideas. Homolytic fission gives radicals, not a carbocation, and this SN2 reaction does not go through a free carbocation intermediate at all.
